title: Freelance Process Playbook Kit
description: Write down the jobs you repeat so they take less time and stop going wrong. Score your tasks to find the five worth documenting first, then use a fill-in procedure template, a one-page checklist template with three filled-in checklists, a complete worked procedure for final delivery and invoicing, ten ready-to-adapt outlines for common freelance processes and a simple routine to keep it all up to date.

files.01-what-to-document-first.md:
# What to Document First

You don't need a procedure for everything. You need one for the handful of tasks where writing it down pays back quickly. This page helps you find them.

## Step 1: list every task you repeat

Open `process-inventory.csv` and write one row per repeat task. Go through these prompts so you don't miss any:

**Winning work**
- Replying to a new enquiry
- Preparing for a discovery call
- Writing and sending a proposal
- Following up on a proposal

**Starting a project**
- Sending the contract and deposit invoice
- Setting up project folders and files
- Sending the welcome email and intake questions
- Running the kickoff call

**Doing the work**
- Your core delivery process (design, writing, development, editing, analysis...)
- Preparing work for client review
- Handling feedback and revisions
- Weekly status update

**Finishing**
- Final delivery and file handover
- Final invoice
- Asking for a testimonial
- Archiving the project

**Running the business**
- Monthly bookkeeping and receipts
- Sending recurring invoices
- Chasing late payments
- Backups
- Updating your portfolio
- Setting aside money for tax
- Planning the next week

## Step 2: score each one

For each task, give a score from 1 to 3 in four columns.

| Column | 1 | 2 | 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Frequency** | A few times a year | Monthly | Weekly or more |
| **Steps** | Under 5 steps | 5-12 steps | More than 12, or several tools |
| **Cost of a mistake** | Mildly annoying | Costs time to fix | Costs money, a deadline or a client's trust |
| **Delegable** | Only you could ever do it | Maybe one day | Someone else could do it with instructions |

**Priority = Frequency + Steps + (Cost of a mistake x 2) + Delegable**

Mistake cost counts double because that's where a procedure earns its keep. The maximum score is 15.

## Step 3: pick your top five

Sort by priority, highest first. Then sanity-check the top five:

- **At least one money process.** Invoicing, chasing payments or monthly bookkeeping. These are where small slips cost you directly.
- **At least one client-facing process.** Onboarding, delivery or status updates. These are where clients notice consistency.
- **Your core delivery process, if it has more than about 10 steps.** It's the one you'd most want to hand off one day, and the one most likely to have steps you skip when tired.

## Step 4: decide the format

| If the task... | Use |
|---|---|
| Has fewer than 10 steps and you already know why each one matters | A one-page checklist (`03-checklist-template.md`) |
| Has decisions ("if the client has X, do Y"), several tools, or would be handed to someone else | A full procedure (`02-sop-template.md`) |
| Is mostly a message you send | An email template, stored with the procedure that triggers it |

## Common traps

- **Documenting what you wish you did.** Write what you actually do, then improve it. An ideal process you never follow is a nice document, not a procedure.
- **Too much detail too soon.** If you'd never forget a step, it doesn't need a line. Add detail only where you, or someone new, would get stuck.
- **Starting with rare tasks.** Your annual review is interesting to write up but you'll use it once a year. Start with what you do every week.
- **Waiting for a quiet month.** Write each procedure the next time you actually do the task, with the procedure open beside the work. It's faster and more accurate than writing from memory.
files.02-sop-template.md:
# Procedure Template

Copy everything below the line into a new document for each process. Fill in the brackets, delete any section that doesn't apply, and keep it as short as it can be while still being followable by someone who isn't you.

A good test: could a capable person who has never worked with you follow this and get it 90% right on the first try? If not, something is missing. If they'd be bored by obvious steps, something can go.

---

# [Process name]

**ID:** [P-03]  **Version:** [1.0]  **Last updated:** [date]  **Owner:** [your name]

## Purpose

[One or two sentences. What this process produces and why it matters.]

Example: *Gets final files to the client in a form they can use without help, and gets the final invoice out the same day so payment isn't delayed.*

## When to use it

- **Trigger:** [what starts this process, e.g. "client approves the final round"]
- **How often:** [e.g. once per project, every Monday, monthly on the 1st]
- **Time it should take:** [e.g. 45 minutes]
- **Done when:** [the finish line, e.g. "files delivered, client confirmed receipt, invoice sent, project folder archived"]

## What you need before starting

- [ ] [Inputs, e.g. "written approval from the client"]
- [ ] [Access, e.g. "login to the client's file storage"]
- [ ] [Information, e.g. "PO number from the contract"]
- [ ] [Templates, e.g. "handover email template, T-07"]

If any of these is missing, [what to do: e.g. "stop and ask the client using email T-04"].

## Tools

| Tool | What it's used for here |
|---|---|
| [File storage] | [Delivery folder] |
| [Invoicing tool or spreadsheet] | [Final invoice] |
| [Email] | [Handover email] |

## Steps

Number every step. Start each with a verb. One action per step.

### Stage 1: [name, e.g. Prepare]

1. [Step]
2. [Step]
   - **Check:** [how you know this step was done right]
3. [Step]
   - **If** [condition], **then** [different action].

### Stage 2: [name, e.g. Deliver]

4. [Step]
5. [Step]
   - **Watch out:** [the mistake people make here]

### Stage 3: [name, e.g. Close]

6. [Step]
7. [Step]

## Quality check

Before calling it done, confirm:

- [ ] [The most important outcome, e.g. "client can open every file"]
- [ ] [The most common miss, e.g. "invoice includes PO number"]
- [ ] [Anything that would be embarrassing if wrong]

## If something goes wrong

| Problem | What to do |
|---|---|
| [e.g. Client can't open a file] | [e.g. Re-export in the alternative format listed in step 3; reply within 4 working hours] |
| [e.g. Client asks for changes after approval] | [e.g. Use the change request process, P-07. Don't edit the delivered files.] |
| [e.g. Payment details bounce] | [e.g. Call the client; never send new bank details by email alone] |

## Related

- Templates: [T-07 handover email]
- Next process: [P-09 project archive]
- Previous process: [P-05 final review round]

## Change history

| Version | Date | What changed | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1.0 | [date] | First version | |

---

## Writing tips

- **Use the words on the screen.** "Click **Share**, then **Anyone with the link**" beats "share the folder publicly". If a tool changes its buttons, update the step.
- **Put the reason next to the risky step.** "Export as PDF/X so print colours match" helps a future you resist skipping it.
- **Make decisions explicit.** "If the client is VAT registered..." or "If the project was over 20 hours..." Hidden decisions are where handovers fail.
- **Link, don't copy.** If an email template or price list lives elsewhere, link to it, so there's only ever one current version.
- **Number the IDs.** P- for procedures, C- for checklists, T- for templates. You'll refer to them in other procedures and it keeps the folder tidy.
files.03-checklist-template.md:
# One-Page Checklist Template

For short, frequent tasks you mostly know by heart but occasionally get wrong. A checklist isn't a training manual. It's a safety net for the steps that are easy to skip when you're busy or tired.

## Rules for a good checklist

1. **5-12 items.** Longer than that and you'll stop reading it. Split it or make it a full procedure.
2. **Only the steps that get missed** or that really matter. Leave out the obvious.
3. **Fits on one screen or one printed page.**
4. **Use it every time,** even when you're sure you remember. That's the point.
5. **Put it where the task happens.** Pinned in the project tool, taped above the desk, saved as a recurring task.

---

## Template

# C-[number]: [Task name]

**Use:** [trigger, e.g. "before sending any invoice"]   **Time:** [e.g. 3 min]   **Updated:** [date]

**Before**
- [ ] [item]
- [ ] [item]

**During**
- [ ] [item]
- [ ] [item]
- [ ] [item]

**After**
- [ ] [item]
- [ ] [item]

**Stop if:** [the one condition that means don't continue, e.g. "no written approval yet"]

---

## Three filled-in examples

### C-01: Before sending any invoice

**Use:** every invoice   **Time:** 3 min

- [ ] Invoice number follows on from the last one
- [ ] Client's legal name and billing address, not just their brand name
- [ ] PO number, if this client uses them
- [ ] Line items match the quote or milestone wording
- [ ] Currency shown next to the total
- [ ] Due date written as a full date
- [ ] Payment details copied from the bank or provider, not retyped
- [ ] Saved as PDF with a clear file name
- [ ] Sent to the accounts email as well as your contact, if they asked
- [ ] Logged in your invoice tracker with the due date

**Stop if:** the work it covers hasn't been approved or the milestone hasn't been reached.

### C-02: Monday planning (15 minutes)

**Use:** every Monday, first thing   **Time:** 15 min

- [ ] Check the calendar for the week: calls, deadlines, personal commitments
- [ ] List every deliverable due this week and next
- [ ] Check what you're waiting on from clients, and nudge anything overdue
- [ ] Check unpaid invoices and chase anything past due
- [ ] Block focused work time for each deliverable
- [ ] Pick the one thing that must get done this week if nothing else does
- [ ] Note any capacity for new work, so you can answer enquiries honestly

**Stop if:** you're double-booked on a deadline. Sort that out with the client today, not on Thursday.

### C-03: Before sending work for client review

**Use:** every review round   **Time:** 5 min

- [ ] Re-read the brief or the last round's feedback; every point addressed?
- [ ] Spell-check and proofread (read it aloud or in a different view)
- [ ] File names are clear and include the round number (`Homepage-v2.pdf`)
- [ ] Links work when you're logged out
- [ ] Review email says what kind of feedback you need and by when
- [ ] Review email says how many revision rounds remain
- [ ] Calendar reminder set for the feedback due date

**Stop if:** you're sending it just to hit a date and you know it isn't ready. Send a short "one more day" note instead.
files.04-worked-example.md:
# Worked Example: Final Delivery and Invoice

This is a complete procedure written by a fictional freelance brand designer, **Tomás**, who makes logos and small brand identity packs for independent businesses. It's here to show the level of detail that works: enough that an assistant could follow it, not so much that it's tedious.

Tomás wrote version 1.0 from memory. He then used it on his next project and fixed three things straight afterwards (see the change history at the end). That second version is the one shown.

---

# P-08: Final Delivery and Invoice

**ID:** P-08  **Version:** 1.1  **Last updated:** 3 March 2027  **Owner:** Tomás

## Purpose

Gets the client a complete, well-organised set of brand files they can use without asking for help, and gets the final invoice out the same day. Clients who can find and open everything don't send "where's the..." emails three months later, and invoices sent on delivery day get paid faster.

## When to use it

- **Trigger:** client approves the final round in writing (email or comment saying "approved" or equivalent)
- **How often:** once per project, about 2-3 times a month
- **Time it should take:** 60-75 minutes
- **Done when:** files delivered, client confirmed they can open them, final invoice sent and logged, project folder archived

## What you need before starting

- [ ] Written final approval, saved to the project folder as `approval.pdf` or a screenshot
- [ ] The final approved design files
- [ ] Project contract or proposal, for the deliverables list and payment terms
- [ ] Client's legal name, billing address and PO number (in the client info sheet)
- [ ] Templates: T-11 handover email, T-12 brand guide one-pager

If written approval is missing: stop. Send T-10 ("ready to finalise?") and wait. Never export finals on a verbal OK.

## Tools

| Tool | Used for |
|---|---|
| Design software | Exporting final files |
| Cloud file storage | Delivery folder and share link |
| Spreadsheet invoice template | Final invoice |
| Invoice tracker (spreadsheet) | Logging the invoice and due date |
| Email | Handover and invoice emails |

## Steps

### Stage 1: Prepare the files (35-45 min)

1. **Open the proposal** and copy the deliverables list into a new note. This is the checklist for what goes in the folder.
2. **Create the delivery folder** in cloud storage, named `[Client] Brand Files [YYYY-MM]`, with these subfolders:
   - `01 Logo - for print`
   - `02 Logo - for screen`
   - `03 Colours and fonts`
   - `04 Brand guide`
   - `05 Source files` (only if the contract includes source files)
3. **Export every logo version** listed in the proposal (usually: main, stacked, icon only, one-colour) in:
   - Print: PDF and EPS, CMYK
   - Screen: PNG (transparent background) at 500, 1000 and 2000 px wide, and SVG
   - **Watch out:** check transparent PNGs on a dark background before saving. A white box behind the logo is the most common delivery error.
4. **Name files consistently:** `[client]-logo-[version]-[colour]-[format]`, all lowercase, no spaces. Example: `harbourbakery-logo-stacked-white-rgb.png`.
5. **Fill in the brand guide one-pager** (T-12): logo versions with do and don't examples, colour values (HEX, RGB, CMYK), font names and where to get them, minimum logo size.
6. **Export the brand guide as PDF** into `04 Brand guide`.
7. **If the contract includes source files,** save the working design files into `05 Source files` with fonts listed in a `fonts.txt` file. Don't include font files; the client needs their own licence. Explain this in the handover email.
8. **Tick off every item** in the deliverables note from step 1. Anything missing, go back and export it.
   - **Check:** the folder contains everything in the proposal and nothing that isn't (no rejected concepts, no drafts).

### Stage 2: Test the delivery (10 min)

9. **Set sharing** to "anyone with the link can view and download".
10. **Open the link in a private browser window** while logged out. Download the whole folder as a zip and open three random files.
    - **If** anything fails to open or looks wrong, fix it before going on.
11. **Check the link has no expiry date** (or set it to at least 90 days and say so in the email).

### Stage 3: Hand over (10 min)

12. **Send the handover email** (T-11) with:
    - the folder link
    - a two-line guide to which folder to use for what ("print folder for anything your printer asks for; screen folder for your website and social media")
    - the font licence note, if source files are included
    - a request to confirm they can open everything
13. **Set a reminder** for 2 working days to check they've confirmed.

### Stage 4: Invoice (10 min)

14. **Create the final invoice** from the template. Use the milestone wording from the proposal exactly ("Final payment: brand identity pack, 50% balance").
15. **Run checklist C-01** (before sending any invoice).
16. **Send the invoice** in a separate email from the handover, so it's easy for the client to forward to their accounts team. Subject: `Invoice [number]: [project name]`.
17. **Log it** in the invoice tracker with the due date.

### Stage 5: Close (5 min)

18. **When the client confirms receipt,** reply with thanks and, if the project went well, ask for a testimonial (T-14).
19. **Move the project folder** to `Archive/[year]/`. Keep the approval file, contract, final files and invoice together.
20. **Mark the project closed** in the project tracker.

## Quality check

- [ ] Client can download and open everything from a logged-out browser
- [ ] Every deliverable from the proposal is present, nothing extra
- [ ] Transparent PNGs checked on a dark background
- [ ] Invoice includes PO number and matches the proposal wording
- [ ] Invoice logged with due date

## If something goes wrong

| Problem | What to do |
|---|---|
| Client can't open EPS or SVG files | Normal on some computers. Tell them the PNG and PDF versions cover most uses; the EPS and SVG are for their printer or web developer. |
| Client asks for a new logo version after delivery | If it's in the proposal, it was missed: export it the same day and apologise briefly. If not, use P-07 (change request) and quote it. |
| Client asks for the rejected concepts | Not included unless agreed. Offer them as a paid add-on if you're comfortable with that. |
| No confirmation after 2 working days | Send a two-line nudge. After 5 working days, treat delivery as accepted per the contract and note the date. |
| Invoice unpaid after the due date | Follow P-12 (late payment). |

## Related

- Previous: P-07 Change requests, P-06 Final review round
- Next: P-12 Late payment, P-14 Portfolio update
- Templates: T-10, T-11, T-12, T-14
- Checklist: C-01

## Change history

| Version | Date | What changed | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1.0 | 14 February 2027 | First version | Written from memory |
| 1.1 | 3 March 2027 | Added step 3 "watch out" note on transparent PNGs | Delivered a white-box PNG to a client on the first live run |
| 1.1 | 3 March 2027 | Split invoice into a separate email (step 16) | Client said their accounts team missed the invoice inside the handover email |
| 1.1 | 3 March 2027 | Added step 7 font licence note | Client asked why the fonts didn't install with the source files |

---

## What to notice

- **It starts with the trigger and the "stop" rule.** The most expensive mistake in final delivery is exporting before written approval. It's caught before step 1.
- **Each stage has a time.** When delivery takes two hours instead of one, Tomás can see which stage swelled.
- **"Watch out" notes are where he got burned.** Every one came from a real mistake.
- **It points to other procedures** (P-07, P-12) instead of repeating them.
- **Version 1.1 came from one real use.** That's normal. Plan to fix your procedures after the first run.
files.05-starter-outlines.md:
# Ten Starter Outlines

These are skeletons for the processes most freelancers repeat. Each has the trigger, the finish line, the main steps and the mistakes that usually slip through. Copy one into `02-sop-template.md`, then edit the steps to match how you actually work and add your own tools and templates.

---

## P-01: New enquiry to booked call

**Trigger:** a new enquiry arrives (email, contact form, referral, message)
**Done when:** call booked, or a polite "not a fit" sent
**Target:** reply within one working day

1. Log the enquiry in your pipeline tracker (name, source, date, what they asked for).
2. Quick fit check: is it work you do, roughly in your price range, in a timeframe you can meet?
3. **If not a fit:** send your "not a fit" reply, with a referral if you have one. Log as closed.
4. **If a fit:** reply with two or three call slots or your booking link, and your pre-call questions.
5. When booked, add the call to your calendar with their answers attached.
6. Set a follow-up reminder for 3 working days if they don't book.

**Commonly missed:** logging the source (you'll want it when you decide where to spend marketing time); the follow-up reminder.

---

## P-02: Proposal to signed contract

**Trigger:** discovery call finished and the client wants a proposal
**Done when:** contract signed and deposit invoice sent, or proposal closed as lost

1. Write notes from the call within the same day.
2. Draft the proposal from your template: goals, scope, deliverables, timeline, price, payment terms, what's not included.
3. Check the price against your rate maths and capacity.
4. Send with a clear validity date and next step.
5. Follow up after 3 working days, then after 7.
6. On acceptance: send the contract, then the deposit invoice once it's signed.
7. Book the start date in your calendar only when the deposit is paid.

**Commonly missed:** the "not included" list; a validity date; booking time before the deposit lands.

---

## P-03: Client onboarding

**Trigger:** deposit paid
**Done when:** client has everything they need from you, and you have everything you need from them

1. Create the project folder from your folder template.
2. Create the project in your task tool with all milestones and due dates.
3. Send the welcome email: what happens next, how to reach you, your working hours, what you need from them and by when.
4. Send or share the intake questionnaire.
5. Book the kickoff call.
6. Request access to anything you need (accounts, files, brand assets).
7. Add client details (legal name, billing address, PO process, accounts contact) to your client info sheet.

**Commonly missed:** asking about the invoicing process at the start, not at the first invoice; asking who has final sign-off.

---

## P-04: Weekly client update

**Trigger:** every [Friday]
**Done when:** every active client has an update

1. For each active project: what was done this week, what's next week, anything you're waiting on from them, any risks to the timeline.
2. Mark overall status: on track, at risk, or off track.
3. Send. Keep it under 150 words where you can.
4. Note anything you're waiting on in your tracker with a chase date.

**Commonly missed:** naming exactly what you need from the client and by when.

---

## P-05: Review rounds and feedback

**Trigger:** work ready for client review
**Done when:** consolidated feedback received and logged

1. Run checklist C-03 (before sending work for review).
2. Send with: what to review, the kind of feedback you need, the due date, rounds remaining.
3. Log the round in your revision tracker.
4. When feedback arrives, consolidate it into one numbered list and confirm it back to the client.
5. Mark anything that's outside scope and handle it as a change request (quote it before doing it).

**Commonly missed:** confirming your understanding of the feedback before starting changes; saying how many rounds remain.

---

## P-06: Monthly invoicing

**Trigger:** [1st working day] of each month, or each milestone reached
**Done when:** every billable item invoiced and logged

1. List every client with billable work last month (hours, milestones, retainers, expenses).
2. For hourly work, export and check the timesheet.
3. Create each invoice and run checklist C-01.
4. Send, then log in the invoice tracker with due dates.
5. Check last month's invoices: anything overdue goes to P-07 (late payment).

**Commonly missed:** billable expenses; retainer overage hours.

---

## P-07: Late payment follow-up

**Trigger:** an invoice is past its due date
**Done when:** paid, or escalated to your final step

1. Day 1 after due: check your bank or payment account first, then send a friendly reminder.
2. Day 7: second reminder, copy the accounts email, attach the invoice again.
3. Day 14: phone or video call; ask when payment will be made and confirm in writing.
4. Day 21: pause further work if your terms allow, and say so clearly and politely.
5. Day 30: final notice with the next step your terms allow.
6. Log every contact with date and outcome.

**Commonly missed:** checking whether it's already been paid before chasing; logging the dates.

(The numbers here are only a suggestion. The worked example in `04-worked-example.md` uses its own numbering, with P-07 for change requests and P-12 for late payment. Pick one scheme for your playbook and keep to it.)

---

## P-08: Project close and archive

**Trigger:** final invoice paid
**Done when:** project archived and lessons recorded

1. Confirm everything has been delivered and the final invoice is paid.
2. Send a thank-you note and, if it went well, ask for a testimonial or referral.
3. Remove your access to client accounts you no longer need, or ask them to.
4. Move the project folder to the archive.
5. Note actual hours against the quote, and one thing to do differently.
6. Add to your portfolio list if you have permission.

**Commonly missed:** comparing hours to the quote (your best pricing data); removing access.

---

## P-09: Monthly money admin

**Trigger:** [last Friday] of each month
**Done when:** books up to date, tax set aside, next month's cash visible

1. Download bank and payment provider statements.
2. Match every income line to an invoice.
3. Record expenses and save receipts to your receipts folder.
4. Move your tax set-aside percentage into a separate account.
5. Update your cash flow forecast for the next 2-3 months.
6. Note anything to ask your accountant.

**Commonly missed:** receipts for small online subscriptions; the tax transfer.

---

## P-10: Backups

**Trigger:** [every Friday] and before any big software or device change
**Done when:** current work exists in at least two places, one off-site

1. Check your automatic cloud sync ran without errors this week.
2. Run your second backup (external drive or second cloud service).
3. Once a month: restore one random file from the backup to prove it works.
4. Check client files you're contractually required to delete are deleted.

**Commonly missed:** testing a restore; email and invoices (not just project files).
files.06-keeping-it-useful.md:
# Keeping the Playbook Useful

Most process documents die the same way: written once with good intentions, never opened again, gradually wrong. These habits keep yours alive with about 20 minutes a month.

## 1. Organise it so you can find anything in 30 seconds

A simple folder structure works for most freelancers:

```
Playbook/
  00 Index.md
  01 Winning work/
     P-01 New enquiry to booked call.md
     P-02 Proposal to signed contract.md
  02 Starting projects/
     P-03 Client onboarding.md
  03 Delivery/
     P-04 Weekly client update.md
     P-05 Review rounds.md
  04 Finishing/
     P-08 Project close and archive.md
  05 Money/
     P-06 Monthly invoicing.md
     P-07 Late payment.md
     P-09 Monthly money admin.md
  06 Admin/
     P-10 Backups.md
  Checklists/
     C-01 Before sending any invoice.md
     C-02 Monday planning.md
  Templates/
     T-01 Not a fit reply.md
     T-11 Handover email.md
  improvement-log.csv
```

The index is one page: every procedure, checklist and template by ID, name and trigger. If you only open one file, open that.

## 2. Use it at the moment of work

A procedure only helps if it's open while you do the task.

- **Recurring tasks:** put the procedure link inside the recurring calendar event or task. "Monthly invoicing: open P-06."
- **Project stages:** build your project template in your task tool so each stage links to its procedure.
- **Checklists:** pin them where the work happens, or print the two or three you use daily.

## 3. Fix it straight after you use it

The moment right after finishing a task is when you remember what was unclear. Take two minutes:

1. Did you skip or reorder any step? Update the procedure to match reality, or note why the procedure is right and you were wrong.
2. Did anything go wrong? Add a "watch out" note to the step.
3. Did you look something up? Add it, or a link to it.

Record each change in `improvement-log.csv`. Over time the log shows you where your business keeps tripping up.

## 4. The monthly 20-minute review

Once a month, on a fixed day:

- [ ] Read the improvement log entries from the last month.
- [ ] Any problem logged twice or more? Fix the procedure properly, not just with a note.
- [ ] Any procedure you didn't use at all? Either you didn't need it, or you forgot it existed. Decide which.
- [ ] Any tool, price, template or policy changed? Update every procedure that mentions it.
- [ ] Bump version numbers and dates on anything you edited.

## 5. Every six months: the full pass

- Re-score `process-inventory.csv`. Your priorities change as your business does.
- Write the next two or three procedures from the list.
- Delete procedures for things you no longer do. Old procedures that look current are worse than none.

## 6. Handing a procedure to someone else

When you first give a procedure to an assistant, subcontractor or cover person:

1. **Walk through it together once,** with them doing the task and you watching.
2. **Ask them to mark every point they hesitated.** Those are your gaps.
3. **Agree which decisions they can make** and which they must check with you. Write this into the procedure as "**If** ... **then** ask [name]".
4. **Review the first three runs** they do alone, then step back.
5. **Keep confidential client details out of the procedure itself.** Link to where they're stored, with access only for the people who need it.

## Signs the playbook is working

- Routine tasks take less time than they did three months ago.
- The same mistake doesn't happen twice.
- You can take a week off and come back without a "what was I doing?" morning.
- You'd be comfortable handing at least one task to someone else tomorrow.

## Signs it needs attention

- You "know" a step is outdated but haven't changed it.
- You never open the index.
- The improvement log hasn't had an entry in two months, and you're still busy. Things are going wrong; they're just not being written down.

# Freelance Process Playbook Kit

You do the same jobs over and over: setting up a new client, sending the monthly invoice, delivering final files, closing a project. Each time you rebuild the steps from memory, and each time something small slips: a missed attachment, a forgotten backup, an invoice sent without the PO number.

A process playbook is a short set of written checklists for the jobs you repeat. It makes routine work faster, cuts the small mistakes that cost you goodwill, and means you could hand a task to an assistant or subcontractor, or come back from two weeks off, without everything living in your head.

This kit helps you write your first five in a weekend, and keep them useful after that.

## What's inside

| File | What it does | Time |
|---|---|---|
| `01-what-to-document-first.md` | Find the processes worth writing down, and score them | 30 min |
| `02-sop-template.md` | A fill-in template for a full step-by-step procedure | 20-40 min per process |
| `03-checklist-template.md` | A lighter one-page checklist for short, frequent tasks | 10 min per task |
| `04-worked-example.md` | A complete, filled-in procedure for delivering a project and invoicing | 10 min read |
| `05-starter-outlines.md` | Ten common freelance processes, already outlined, ready to adapt | 5-15 min each |
| `06-keeping-it-useful.md` | How to test, improve and organise the playbook so you actually use it | 15 min |
| `process-inventory.csv` | List and score every repeat task (example rows included) | 30 min |
| `improvement-log.csv` | Record what went wrong and what you changed | 2 min per entry |

## The weekend plan

**Saturday morning (1.5 hours)**
1. Read `01-what-to-document-first.md`.
2. Fill in `process-inventory.csv` with every task you repeat. Aim for 15-30 rows.
3. Score them and pick your top five.

**Saturday afternoon (2 hours)**
4. Read `04-worked-example.md` to see the level of detail that works.
5. Write your top process using `02-sop-template.md`, starting from the matching outline in `05-starter-outlines.md` if there is one.
6. Write the next two.

**Sunday (1.5 hours)**
7. Turn any very short, frequent tasks into one-page checklists with `03-checklist-template.md`.
8. Set up the folder structure in `06-keeping-it-useful.md`.
9. Put a reminder in your calendar for the first review in four weeks.

Then use each one the next time you do the task, and fix it straight afterwards. That first live run is where most of the improvement happens.

## Where to keep it

Anywhere you'll actually open it: a folder of documents, a notes app, a project management tool, or printed in a binder. The format matters far less than being able to find the right procedure in under 30 seconds.

## Opening the files

The `.md` files are plain text and open in any text editor, notes app or word processor. The `.csv` files open in Excel, Google Sheets, Numbers or LibreOffice.

## License

For your own freelance business. Edit and use the templates freely, including sharing your finished procedures with people who work with you. Please don't resell or share the kit itself.
